Project 01 · Group Project · MSc Engineering Design · Loughborough

MedMoto:
Emergency Medical Vehicle
for Sub-Saharan Africa

A user-centred design engineering project applying Quality Function Deployment and Value Analysis to develop a low-cost, all-terrain medical transport vehicle deployable in resource-limited African contexts.

Type
Group Project (MSc)
Institution
Loughborough University
Methods
QFD · Value Analysis · Concept Design
Deliverable
Detailed Design Proposal + Drawings

The Problem

In many Sub-Saharan African regions, emergency medical response is severely constrained by infrastructure. Unpaved roads, water crossings, deep mud, and limited fuel supply mean conventional ambulances simply cannot reach patients in time.

The brief required a vehicle capable of transporting a patient on a stretcher across rough, partially-submerged, and off-road terrain while storing medical supplies securely and remaining maintainable at low cost with minimal specialist tooling.

The design team applied a structured QFD process to translate these operational realities into ranked engineering requirements, ensuring every design decision was traceable back to a documented user need.

Individual Contributions

Concept sketches: All five concept ideation sketches (Concepts A–E) were individually produced.
QFD & Objective Tree: Contributed to the House of Quality and the objective tree.
Value Analysis: Individual analytical work on component-level cost–performance optimisation.

Ideation Phase · 5 Concepts Developed

Concept Development

Five distinct concepts were developed and sketched before QFD analysis was used to select and refine the final direction. Each addressed the core tension between off-road capability, patient carrying capacity, and cost.

Concept C: 4-wheel cargo trike with mid-engine and canvas shelter
Concept E: Motorcycle sidecar with dedicated stretcher pod
Tracked vehicle variant: overhead mesh storage, hinge doors
3-wheel variant: canvas cover, coil suspension, railed chassis

Quality Function Deployment

House of Quality · Customer Requirements Ranked Against Engineering Parameters
5/5

Patient Transport Capability

Must carry a full-size patient on a basket stretcher. Highest customer importance rating. This directly drove stretcher storage geometry and lashing hook specification.

5/5

Off-Road Terrain Performance

Must traverse mud, rough ground, and partial water submersion. Required off-road tyre specification, minimum ground clearance 200mm+, and coil suspension travel.

5/5

100cc Engine + Auto Transmission

Low maintenance, widely available across Sub-Saharan Africa, and usable by non-specialist drivers under stress. Highest technical importance score: 50.

5/5

Secure Medical Supply Storage

Supplies must survive rough terrain without displacement. Velcro straps, locking doors, and under-stretcher storage zones were all specified from this requirement.

3/5

Long Range / Fuel Capacity

Technical importance score: 42. Drove fuel tank sizing and engine selection, balancing range against weight penalty. Resolved via engine efficiency rather than tank volume.

3/5

Easy to Maintain

Standard parts, widely available tools, and accessible components. This requirement eliminated complex proprietary systems and informed the choice of a standard motorcycle base.

Final Design · Selected Concept Developed to Detail

Final Design Output

The selected concept, a motorcycle-sidecar configuration based on an existing 100cc engine platform, was developed to assembly drawing level. The sidecar carries the stretcher pod and medical storage box as modular components.

Final assembled view: motorcycle base and sidecar stretcher module
Exploded view: chassis, stretcher pod, medical storage, spare wheel
Front view: stretcher canopy open position, chassis connection points

Value Analysis: Component Optimisation

A formal value analysis was conducted on three components where cost reduction and performance improvement were identified as achievable simultaneously. Each component was systematically evaluated against the questions: Can it be eliminated? What costs less but performs as well? Can two parts become one?

Stretcher Support

Original: aluminium formed support. Required machining, custom fabrication, high unit cost.

Hard plastic moulding + cargo net overlay
All criteria met ✓
~£100 plastic moulding
Reduced ✓
Aluminium Storage Box

Original: fully enclosed aluminium box with cover. Heavy, expensive, access limited.

Hard plastic shallow case + hinge side door
All criteria met ✓
~£10 door panel only
Reduced ✓

Project 02 · Personal Project · Early-Stage Ideation

AirHarvest:
Wind Energy from
Train Tunnels

A self-initiated conceptual design project exploring the recovery of kinetic energy from the high-velocity airflows generated by trains moving through enclosed tunnel systems, converting wasted aerodynamic energy into usable electricity.

Early-Stage Ideation
Personal R&D Project
Energy Harvesting · Piezoelectric · EM Generation
⚙ Preliminary Ideation Stage

The Opportunity

Every train passing through a tunnel generates a powerful, predictable pressure wave and high-velocity airstream. This energy is currently dissipated entirely as heat and turbulence. That represents a substantial and consistent energy source that is completely untapped.

Urban metro systems and mainline rail tunnels experience multiple train passages per hour at speeds generating localised airflows of 30–80 km/h. The regularity and predictability of this source distinguishes it from ambient wind, making purpose-designed harvesting devices viable where conventional wind turbines would not be.

Design Question

"Can a compact, maintenance-free device be mounted within an operational tunnel to continuously harvest and convert train-induced airflow into usable electrical energy?"

Two competing conversion mechanisms were explored at concept level, each offering a different trade-off between mechanical complexity, output voltage, and scalability.

Concept 1: Piezoelectric Approach

Wind Wheel + Piezo Patches

A cylindrical wind wheel (rotor) is driven by the tunnel airflow. As the wheel rotates, spaced magnet patches on an end disc interact with piezoelectric patches mounted in the housing, mechanically straining the piezo elements to generate alternating voltage with each pass.

No sliding electrical contacts, magnetically actuated patches only
Generates AC voltage, requires rectification and conditioning
Output scales with rotational speed and number of piezo elements
Low voltage output, better suited to sensor and monitoring power than grid supply

Key design challenge: matching piezo element resonant frequency to expected actuation frequency at tunnel airflow velocities.

Concept 2: Electromagnetic Approach

Rotor + EM Generator

A conventional electromagnetic generator is driven by the same wind wheel rotor. Piezoelectric beams are incorporated radially within the rotor disc, deflecting as the rotor spins to provide supplementary power output in addition to the main EM generation.

Higher power output than piezo-only approach
Conventional generator technology, well-understood and serviceable
Hybrid output: main EM AC + supplementary piezo AC
More mechanical complexity: bearings, shaft, and coil winding required

Key design challenge: packaging a robust EM generator within tunnel installation constraints while managing heat generated in the casing.

Energy Source Characterisation

Train-induced airflow is periodic, predictable, and high-velocity, fundamentally different from ambient wind. Design parameters must account for pulse duration (seconds per train passage) versus continuous flow assumptions in conventional wind turbine design.

Conversion Mechanism Trade-off

Piezoelectric harvesting offers simplicity and no rotating contacts, but voltage output is low (milliwatts to low watts). Electromagnetic generation is higher output but mechanically more complex. Hybrid approaches may optimise both.

Installation Constraint Thinking

The device must be mountable in an operational tunnel environment. That means vibration-resistant, low-profile to fit clearance gauge, maintenance-minimal, and capable of surviving the pressure waves of passing trains as both a wind source and a structural load case.

Identified Next Steps

If this project were to be developed further, the following stages would constitute a systematic design development pathway:

01

CFD Airflow Modelling

Characterise actual tunnel airflow velocities, pressure profiles, and pulse durations using CFD simulation of representative train/tunnel geometries to establish real input parameters.

02

Power Output Estimation

Betz limit analysis and piezoelectric constitutive modelling to estimate achievable output per device. Size the generator and storage to a realistic application (tunnel sensor network, LED lighting).

03

Prototype & Test

Build a bench-scale prototype of the wind wheel + generator assembly. Test under controlled airflow conditions using a wind tunnel or fan rig to validate conversion efficiency and structural integrity.

Project 03 · Professional R&D · InnovateUK-Funded Programme

Ceramic Separators
for Solid-State Batteries

An applied R&D programme developing precision ceramic separator components for next-generation solid-state batteries, progressed from early feasibility through prototype validation as part of an InnovateUK-funded consortium at AM-COE.

Type
Industrial R&D Programme
Funding
InnovateUK
Sector
Energy Storage · Solid-State Batteries
Maturity
TRL 2 → TRL 4
The Brief

Ceramic Structures at Sub-Millimetre Precision

Solid-state batteries need ceramic separator structures with controlled porosity, tight dimensional tolerances, and reliable thermal and structural behaviour. The programme set out to develop a workable material and manufacturing route that could deliver these components repeatably, from early formulation through prototype validation.

I joined the programme as part of the product development team, focused on the material development side of the work. Geometry, deposition setup, and preliminary manufacturing planning all fed into the same research effort.

My Role

Material Formulation and DLP Setup Design

My central technical work was formulating ceramic slurries loaded with a conductive component from the family of solid electrolyte ceramics used in next-generation battery chemistries. This ran alongside material trade-off analysis to balance thermal, structural, and porosity requirements.

I also contributed to the design of the deposition setup we used on our DLP printers, iterating on parameter combinations such as scraper application versus pressing the ceramic material between two films to hit our target printed layer thickness of around one millimetre. Simple mechanical measurements of printed thickness, geometry decisions as part of the research process, and preliminary planning of what the wider manufacturing flow could look like once the material chemistry was settled all sat within our remit. Electrochemical performance testing on printed samples was carried out in partnership with external research institutes. Design and material development records were maintained across the programme to support formal reviews.

Material Development at the Core

The central technical work was formulation. Developing ceramic slurries with a solid electrolyte component that would print reliably on our DLP setup and behave predictably once processed. Every downstream decision, from deposition setup to sample testing, tied back to material chemistry.

Precision Under Constraint

Hitting a target printed layer thickness of around one millimetre on a solid electrolyte ceramic slurry meant designing with process behaviour in mind. Material composition, deposition method, and print parameters all fed back into each other rather than being treated in isolation.

Multi-Stakeholder Delivery

Programme delivery involved coordination across an industrial client, InnovateUK reporting cadence, and internal materials and process specialists. Decisions on formulation, deposition setup, and geometry required alignment across all parties while holding tight to the funded milestone schedule.

What This Project Represents

Why this work matters in the context of a design engineering career:

01

Emerging Technology Contribution

Solid-state batteries are a strategically important UK technology area. Contributing to InnovateUK-funded work in this space reflects both technical capability and comfort with early-TRL engineering under uncertainty.

02

Precision and Process, Integrated

Material formulation, deposition setup design, geometry, and testing all sat within one integrated research effort. Progress on any one of them required movement in the others, which is how the design engineering discipline shows up in practice on early-stage work.
